title: Songbook and Bakery
premise: For ten years, Freya Almeida has written anonymous letters to the soldier she loved and lost, mailing them to an address that stopped answering long ago. When Elias Vane—the man those letters were meant for, and the father of her daughter—moves into the apartment above her bakery-neighbor's shop, she realizes he never received a single letter: they were intercepted and destroyed by his mother, who believed Freya's small-town life would ruin his military career. As the autumn bread festival forces them together, Elias pieces together the truth of the daughter he never knew, while Freya must decide whether a decade of rehearsed silence is worth more than one spoken sentence. On the festival's final night, she finally says it—'I never stopped choosing you'—and they begin, deliberately and imperfectly, again.
about_author: Wendell Blackwood is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who spent fifteen years recommending other people's love stories before writing one. He lives above a bakery, insists the smell of yeast is the only acceptable alarm clock, and answers letters—always.

chapters.title: The Weight of Unsigned Paper
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Opening on a rainy Tuesday, Freya seals her 117th unsent letter and hides it in the bookshop's false drawer, then opens the shop to her daughter June and the regulars who know everything and say nothing. Emotional beat: tender routine masking a decade of grief, establishing what she's afraid to want.

chapters.title: Moving Vans and Cinnamon
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias arrives in Harbor Row with two duffel bags and a medical discharge he hasn't told his mother about, renting the flat above Marguerite's bakery. He recognizes Freya across the street and freezes. Emotional beat: the shock of proximity—home is not the refuge he planned.

chapters.title: Regulars and Rumors
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The town gossips about the returning soldier; Freya pretends indifference while June, ten years old and sharp, asks why a stranger looked at her 'like a math problem.' Emotional beat: the first crack in Freya's careful invisibility.

chapters.title: Coffee, Overdue
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias comes to the bookshop to return a book he never borrowed—Marguerite's meddling—and the conversation between him and Freya is polite, loaded, and ten years too late. He notices June's eyes. Emotional beat: dread and hope colliding over a checkout counter.

chapters.title: The Festival Committee
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya is drafted into organizing the autumn bread festival, which means weeks of meetings with Elias, who volunteers to escape his mother's phone calls. Emotional beat: forced proximity turning antagonism-tinged awkwardness into something warmer.

chapters.title: Letters He Never Got
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Sorting his late grandmother's estate, Elias finds one of Freya's letters she'd once slipped into his duffel before deployment—unopened. He reads it in one sitting and understands what was taken from them. Emotional beat: grief reframed; the past reopens.

chapters.title: June's Questions
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. June, having noticed Elias's resemblance in the shop mirror, asks the question Freya has rehearsed answers to for a decade: 'Do I have a dad?' Freya gives a partial truth and hates herself for it. Emotional beat: motherhood versus honesty; the cost of protection.

chapters.title: Flour on His Hands
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias helps Marguerite bake for the festival and, clumsy and earnest, asks her about Freya's life these ten years. Marguerite tells him almost everything, including June's birthday. Emotional beat: the arithmetic of absence becoming undeniable.

chapters.title: The Mother's Visit
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Helena Vane arrives unannounced, polished and controlling, pushing Elias toward a Boston job and away from Harbor Row. She sees June outside the bookshop and goes pale. Emotional beat: the antagonist's motive revealed—she knew, and she chose his career over his family.

chapters.title: Almost Told
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. On the festival's midway setup night, Elias and Freya share cider and he starts to say something about June; Freya, terrified, cuts him off with logistics and leaves. Emotional beat: self-sabotage—the sentence she's rehearsed for a decade stuck behind her teeth.

chapters.title: The False Drawer, Opened
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. June, shelving books after school, accidentally opens the false drawer and finds the letters—addressed to her father, in her mother's hand. She reads three before Freya catches her. Emotional beat: the secret detonates from inside the family.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Closing Time
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Elias arrives having heard from June; the confrontation is raw—ten years, 117 letters, a daughter, a lie by omission on both sides. Freya admits she stopped mailing them after year three. Emotional beat: anger that is really heartbreak; both retreat wounded.

chapters.title: Helena's Version
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Helena confesses she intercepted and burned every letter Freya sent, showing him the one she kept as leverage. Elias sees the architecture of his lost decade and orders her out. Emotional beat: betrayal clarified; loyalty to his mother finally breaks.

chapters.title: June Runs
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Feeling like a plot twist in her own life, June skips school and is found at the harbor by Elias, who sits with her for two hours and doesn't explain anything—just stays. Emotional beat: the first true father-daughter moment, unearned but real.

chapters.title: What the Letters Said
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias reads all 117 letters in one night, watching Freya's voice change from hope to grief to steady, aching endurance. He writes back—letter 118—though he doesn't yet know how to give it to her. Emotional beat: love rebuilt from evidence; resolve hardening.

chapters.title: The Festival Opens
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The bread festival launches; the town watches Freya and Elias orbit each other. Helena appears at the bookshop and offers Freya money to disappear properly this time. Freya refuses—but Helena reveals Elias took the Boston job. Emotional beat: the old wound dressed in new clothes.

chapters.title: Misread and Missing
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Believing Elias chose Boston again, Freya shuts down, tells June nothing, and throws herself into festival logistics. Marguerite, sensing the misunderstanding, tries to intervene and is rebuffed. Emotional beat: the dark night of the soul—old stories masquerading as truth.

chapters.title: Letter 118
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias, who never accepted the Boston offer, learns Freya heard otherwise, and realizes Helena manufactured it. He leaves Letter 118 with June's schoolbag and asks Marguerite for one favor: the festival's closing ceremony. Emotional beat: the counter-move; hope re-entering through the side door.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At the festival's closing, before the whole town, Elias reads Letter 118 aloud—every year he grieved her, every question he has for June. Freya, shaking, finally says the rehearsed sentence: 'I never stopped choosing you.' Emotional beat: the climax—ten years of silence ending in public, trembling truth.

chapters.title: Helena's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Helena, confronted by both Freya and Elias, finally breaks—not into apology, but into the truth of her own fear: that she was nothing without her son's achievements. Elias offers a boundary, not a banishment. Emotional beat: antagonist humanized; duty released, not avenged.

chapters.title: June's Turn
chapters.summary: June's POV. June interrogates Elias over pancakes—hard questions, kid logic, a trial with a verdict. She asks him to walk her to school, not as a father, but as 'someone practicing.' Emotional beat: forgiveness as a process, granted in increments; the family's youngest sets its terms.

chapters.title: Second Editions
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Weeks later, Freya mails Letter 118's reply to no address at all—she hands it to Elias in person. The bookshop adds a shelf for 'second editions'; the bakery below smells of cinnamon; the festival becomes their anniversary. Emotional beat: resolution—love not as a return to the past, but a deliberate new printing.
